title: The Kinase That Needs Both Halves

scenes.tts: How does a kinase know that a lipid has just been cut, here and now? A receptor fires at the cell surface, and an enzyme cuts a lipid in the membrane. The kinase waits in the cytosol. What could tell it?
scenes.visual: A membrane with a row of lipid tickets on top, a folded kinase waiting below. A dashed path of question marks joins the kinase to one lipid. A receptor fires, an enzyme lands on that lipid, and the kinase still has no way to know.
scenes.narration: How does a kinase know that a lipid has just been cut, here and now? A receptor fires at the cell surface, and an enzyme cuts a lipid in the membrane. The kinase waits in the cytosol. What could tell it?

scenes.tts: The lipid is P I P two, on the inside surface of the membrane. The enzyme phospholipase C cuts it, like a ticket torn along its perforation. One half is I P three, with three phosphates, so it dissolves in water and leaves. The other half is D A G, an oil, so it stays in the membrane where it was made. One cut makes two second messengers, in two places.
scenes.caption: The lipid is PIP2, on the inside surface of the membrane. The enzyme phospholipase C cuts it, like a ticket torn along its perforation. One half is IP3, with three phosphates, so it dissolves in water and leaves. The other half is DAG, an oil, so it stays in the membrane where it was made. One cut makes two second messengers, in two places.
scenes.visual: Zoomed in on one lipid: a ticket with an orange tail half in the membrane and a teal head half below it. The enzyme tears it along the dashed line. The teal half collects three phosphates and drifts away; the orange half stays in the membrane.
scenes.narration: The lipid is PIP2, on the inside surface of the membrane. The enzyme phospholipase C cuts it, like a ticket torn along its perforation. One half is IP3, with three phosphates, so it dissolves in water and leaves. The other half is DAG, an oil, so it stays in the membrane where it was made. scenes.tts: Follow the half that left. I P three diffuses to the endoplasmic reticulum, a calcium store inside the cell. A channel in its membrane opens when I P three binds. The store holds free calcium at a thousand times the resting cytosolic level, or more. So an open channel means a fast rise, and D A G stays in the membrane.
scenes.caption: Follow the half that left. IP3 diffuses to the endoplasmic reticulum, a calcium store inside the cell. A channel in its membrane opens when IP3 binds. The store holds free calcium at a thousand times the resting cytosolic level, or more. So an open channel means a fast rise, and DAG stays in the membrane.
scenes.visual: The teal half travels down to the endoplasmic reticulum and docks on a channel in its wall, which swings open. Two bars compare free calcium in the store with the resting cytosol; yellow calcium streams out and the cytosol bar shoots up. The orange half stays in the membrane.
scenes.narration: Follow the half that left. IP3 diffuses to the endoplasmic reticulum, a calcium store inside the cell. A channel in its membrane opens when IP3 binds. The store holds free calcium at a thousand times the resting cytosolic level, or more. So an open channel means a fast rise, and DAG stays in the membrane.

scenes.tts: Now meet the conventional kind of protein kinase C, which puts phosphates on serines and threonines. At rest it is folded shut in the cytosol. A stretch called the pseudosubstrate sits in its active site and blocks it. The C two part lands on the membrane only when it holds calcium. The C one part binds D A G in the membrane.
scenes.caption: Now meet the conventional kind of protein kinase C, which puts phosphates on serines and threonines. At rest it is folded shut in the cytosol. A stretch called the pseudosubstrate sits in its active site and blocks it. The C2 part lands on the membrane only when it holds calcium. The C1 part binds DAG in the membrane.
scenes.visual: The kinase rises into view: a purple body with a notch for its active site, a red plug sitting in the notch, and two arms ending in a yellow C2 hand and an orange C1 hand. A calcium dot docks on C2; a dashed line joins C1 to the DAG in the membrane.
scenes.narration: Now meet the conventional kind of protein kinase C, which puts phosphates on serines and threonines. At rest it is folded shut in the cytosol. A stretch called the pseudosubstrate sits in its active site and blocks it. The C2 part lands on the membrane only when it holds calcium. The C1 part binds DAG in the membrane.

scenes.tts: Each signal alone rises for many reasons. Calcium also rises when a voltage-gated channel opens. With calcium alone, C two holds the membrane weakly, and the kinase stays largely off. Other lipid enzymes also make D. A. G. With D. A. G. alone, C one holds weakly too, and the kinase stays largely off.
scenes.caption: Each signal alone rises for many reasons. Calcium also rises when a voltage-gated channel opens. With calcium alone, C2 holds the membrane weakly, and the kinase stays largely off. Other lipid enzymes also make DAG. With DAG alone, C1 holds weakly too, and the kinase stays largely off.
scenes.visual: Case one: calcium pours through a voltage-gated channel; the C2 hand grabs the membrane and slips off, the plug stays in. Reset. Case two: another lipid enzyme makes DAG; the C1 hand grabs and slips off, the plug stays in.
scenes.narration: Each signal alone rises for many reasons. Calcium also rises when a voltage-gated channel opens. With calcium alone, C2 holds the membrane weakly, and the kinase stays largely off. Other lipid enzymes also make DAG. With DAG alone, C1 holds weakly too, and the kinase stays largely off.

scenes.tts: Each contact is weak alone, but binding energies add, so preferences multiply. Say each contact alone favors the membrane thirtyfold, and the pair favors it about nine hundredfold. Calcium and D A G appear together mainly because phospholipase C has just cut P I P two there. Only then is the kinase held firmly enough to free its active site, so it works as a coincidence detector. So keep this rule: conventional protein kinase C fires only when calcium and D A G arrive together.
scenes.caption: Each contact is weak alone, but binding energies add, so preferences multiply. Say each contact alone favors the membrane thirtyfold, and the pair favors it about nine hundredfold. scenes.visual: Bars show the membrane preference: thirty, thirty, then nine hundred. Then the cut happens above the kinase: the orange half stays, calcium wells up, both hands grip, the plug is pulled out of the active site and the kinase turns green.
